newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU soft drinks industry demands sugar reforms.
newsitem.headline: EU soft drinks industry demands sugar reforms.

text.p: European Union soft drinks producers on Tuesday called for urgent reform of sugar production and marketing rules to prepare for the next round of world trade negotiations and the EU's expansion eastwards.
The EU is expected to come under further pressure to reduce sugar and other farm subsidies, as well as to open its markets when the World Trade Organisation opens farm trade negotiations in 1999.

The prospective membership of up to 10 central and east European countries early next century could also lead to a flood of complaints to the WTO if the EU does not apply world prices in these countries.
"If the EU is unprepared it will have to negotiate with its back to the wall," Alain Beaumont, Secretary General of the Union of EC Soft Drinks Associations (UNESDA), told Reuters in an interview.

Sugar should be reformed along with cereals, beef and milk, added Beaumont, noting that the EU produces an annual sugar surplus of more than four million tonnes that is placed on world markets with the aid of huge subsidies.
UNESDA says the EU sugar regime encourages inefficient sugar producers, at a huge cost to consumers and industrial users.

It wants to uncouple subsidies from production, with EU income support payments made directly to sugar beet farmers. It also wants to abolish national production quotas and ease curbs on the use of cheap sweeteners, such as liquid corn syrup.
Beaumont said it was a myth that a producer levy meant that the EU's sugar regime was self-financing, as the cost, estimated at some 5.8 billion Ecus a year, was passed on to consumers.
"We have a feeling that (EU Farm Commissioner Franz) Fischler believes reform is needed and is throwing the ball into the sugar camp," he said.

But the European Commission has said that there is a lack of political will for reform among the 15 EU member states. It noted that farm ministers agreed in April 1995 to extend the sugar regime for six years with only minor changes.

"If it isn't broken, don't fix it," said a Commission agriculture official, adding that a reduction in sugar support prices was more likely to result in increased profits for soft drinks companies than savings for consumers.

Beaumont said a new report, commissioned by the soft drinks industry, stressed the sensitivity of sugar prices -- around 20 percent of total production costs -- and that growth has only been maintained by keeping prices under the rate of inflation.
"This is despite the additional costs...such as EU controlled sugar prices which have been kept at a level at least double that of free market world prices," said the report by Canadean Ltd.
The report noted that the soft drinks sector is the third largest user of sugar after private consumers and the chocolate industry, taking about three million tonnes annually.
The soft drinks industry was also a source of jobs, employing nearly one million people directly or indirectly.
